name: venmo_voice

_provenance.method: CURATED extraction — fingerprinted from shipped strings, then filtered to voice-bearing. The filter IS the authorship: deciding which strings count as voice is the CD judgment. Not 'just extracted' — curated, and the curation is the value (Wren review 2026-07-16).
_provenance.reading: This is the VOICE (constant — who Venmo is), and it is a BASELINE (descriptive: what Venmo sounds like on average), NOT a target (prescriptive: what good looks like). Shipped != good — a corpus carries legacy / deadline / A-B-loser strings. good_examples must be a CURATED GOLDEN SUBSET, not the whole corpus.
_provenance.why_held: observed / derived — nobody agreed to these rules, they were derived from the corpus. Carry LOWER confidence than authored rules (not why_held:consensus).
_provenance.note: corpus has de-ID concatenation artifacts (eaten spaces: 'findbank', 'createteen'); voice signal unaffected, but clean before using strings verbatim

voice_principles.principle: Second person, always. Talk TO the user, not about them.
voice_principles.evidence: 61% of voice-bearing strings use you/your; the two most common openers are 'Your' (211) and 'You' (173).
examples: You can find your bank account number on your bank statement or check.

voice_principles.principle: The brand is a 'we' that helps — present, doing things alongside you, never a faceless system.
voice_principles.evidence: 18% use we/our; 'We' is the #3 opener (158); the pattern is 'We'll…' (we act on your behalf).
examples: We'll let your parent or guardian know that there's an issue.
If there isn't enough, we'll use your bank to make the full payment.

voice_principles.principle: Plain and short. Clarity over cleverness.
voice_principles.evidence: ~12 words per string on average; 11% imperative (guides, doesn't command).
examples: Log in to your bank account to get things reconnected.

voice_principles.principle: Casual and contracted — friendly, human, not formal.
voice_principles.evidence: 29% of strings use contractions (we'll, you'll, it's).
examples: This is how we'll refer to you and how you'll show up in the app.

voice_principles.principle: Explain the why on friction. When you ask for something sensitive, say why.
voice_principles.evidence: Requests for personal data are paired with a reason rather than a bare demand.
examples: We need your legal name to make sure it's really you.
Your location is necessary to use certain features and see more relevant results.

voice_principles.principle: Reassure, don't alarm. On holds/issues: calm + a next step, never blame.
voice_principles.evidence: Exclamation only 4%; questions only 3% — restrained affect even on problems.
examples: We place holds on payments for different reasons. Please check your notifications or transaction details for more info.

voice_principles.principle: Delight is sparing and earned — a rare whimsical moment, never forced.
voice_principles.evidence: Playful lines are the exception buried among transactional strings, not the default register.
examples: Virtual carrier pigeons delivered your invitations.

avoid: Hype and exclamation-stacking (baseline exclamation is only 4%)
Title Case (sentence case is the norm)
Jargon / formal register (contractions are the norm)
Alarming or blaming tone on holds, errors, and identity checks
Talking ABOUT the user in third person (the voice is second-person)
